solution:
The compound as a whole is neutral. The counter ion outside the coordination sphere is \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}}\), so the complex ion \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Br]}\) must carry a charge of \(+2\).

Inside the sphere \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) is a neutral ligand and \(\mathrm{Br^{\ominus}}\) carries \(-1\). Hence

\(x + 5(0) + (-1) = +2\), so \(x = +3\).

The other values fail on the same balance: \(+2\) would leave the complex ion at \(+1\) and \(+4\) would leave it at \(+3\), neither of which can be neutralised by one divalent sulphate ion, while \(+1\) would make the sphere neutral and no counter ion would be printed at all.

The oxidation state of cobalt is therefore \(+3\).

[Textbook misprint: the keyed option is printed as "bis (ethylenediamine dithiocyanatoplatinum (IV) ion" — the closing parenthesis after "ethylenediamine" is missing, so as set the ligand name runs into the metal name. It is preserved exactly as printed. The chapter's own Table 9.3 gives the correct form, "Bis(ethylenediamine)dithiocyanatoplatinum(IV)". The three distractors carry misprints too, also preserved: "dithiocyantoplatinate" for dithiocyanatoplatinate, "dicyanatobis" for dithiocyanatobis, "ethylenediammine" for ethylenediamine and "dithiocynato" for dithiocyanato. None of them affects the reasoning, which turns on "platinum" versus "platinate".]

This complex is named in the chapter's own Table 9.3 (cationic complexes) as **bis(ethylenediamine)dithiocyanatoplatinum(IV)**.

The reasoning behind that name: the ligands are named first in alphabetical order, \(\mathrm{(en)_2}\) becomes bis(ethylenediamine) because the ligand name itself already contains a numerical prefix, and \(\mathrm{SCN^{\ominus}}\) bound through sulphur is thiocyanato, so dithiocyanato. Since the coordination sphere carries a net \(+2\) charge it is a CATION, and rule 8 of the chapter says the metal keeps its usual name in a cationic complex — the ending 'ate' is reserved for an ANIONIC complex.

That single test eliminates three of the four choices, since they all name the metal 'platinate'. One of them additionally reads dicyanato rather than dithiocyanato, which is a different ligand altogether, and another spells the ligand ethylenediammine.

Only the reading 'bis(ethylenediamine)dithiocyanatoplatinum(IV) ion' survives; it is printed with a misplaced bracket but is the intended name.

[Textbook misprint: the stem prints "hexacynoferrate"; the correct spelling is hexacyanoferrate, as the chapter's own Table 9.3 sets it ("Hexacyanoferrate(II) ion"). Preserved as printed. The intended compound and the answer are unaffected.]

'Ferrate' means the complex ion is anionic and 'hexacyano' means six \(\mathrm{CN^{\ominus}}\) ligands. With iron in the \(+3\) state stated by the Roman numeral,

charge on the complex ion \(= +3 + 6(-1) = -3\), i.e. \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{3\ominus}}\).

Three sodium ions are needed to balance it, giving \(\mathrm{Na_3[Fe(CN)_6]}\).

Testing the rest: \(\mathrm{Na_2[Fe(CN)_6]}\) and \(\mathrm{Na[Fe(CN)_6]}\) would require iron in the \(+4\) and \(+5\) states respectively, and \(\mathrm{[NaFe(CN)_6]}\) puts sodium INSIDE the coordination sphere, which contradicts the name — sodium is written first precisely because it is the counter ion, exactly as in the chapter's \(\mathrm{Na_3[Co(NO_2)_6]}\), sodium hexanitrocobaltate(III).

The formula is \(\mathrm{Na_3[Fe(CN)_6]}\).

[Textbook misprint: options (a) and (c) are printed CHARACTER-FOR-CHARACTER IDENTICAL — both read "1 and 3" — verified on the source page at high magnification. Since "1 and 3" is the correct answer, this question as printed has TWO correct options and a student choosing (c) is right on the chemistry. The options are preserved exactly as printed and the key is recorded on the first of the two identical choices. Almost certainly one of the two was meant to read a different pair, but the book does not say which, so nothing has been invented in its place.]

Cis-trans isomerism needs two identical ligands that can be placed either adjacent or opposite. The chapter states that it is shown by square planar complexes of the \(\mathrm{MA_2B_2}\) and \(\mathrm{MA_2BC}\) types and by octahedral complexes of the \(\mathrm{MA_4B_2}\), \(\mathrm{MA_4BC}\) and \(\mathrm{M(AA)_2B_2}\) types, and that four-coordinate TETRAHEDRAL complexes do not show cis and trans isomers.

Taking the four complexes in turn:

1. \(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_2Cl_4]^{\ominus}}\) — six ligands, so octahedral, of the \(\mathrm{MA_4B_2}\) type with \(\mathrm{A = Cl}\) and \(\mathrm{B = NH_3}\). The two ammine ligands can be adjacent or opposite, so it DOES show cis and trans isomers.

2. \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Br]^{2\oplus}}\) — an \(\mathrm{MA_5B}\) octahedral complex. There is only one bromide, and every one of the six positions is equivalent to every other in an octahedron, so only one arrangement exists. No isomers.

3. \(\mathrm{[PtCl_2Br_2]^{2\ominus}}\) — stated to be square planar, and it is of the \(\mathrm{MA_2B_2}\) type. The two chlorides may be adjacent (cis) or opposite (trans), so it DOES show cis and trans isomers.

4. \(\mathrm{[FeCl_2(NCS)_2]^{2\ominus}}\) — stated to be tetrahedral. In a tetrahedron all four corners are mutually adjacent, so no pair of positions is 'opposite' and the distinction between cis and trans does not arise. No geometric isomers.

So the complexes that exist as cis and trans isomers are 1 and 3.

A chiral complex is one whose mirror image is non-superimposable on it. The chapter shows that the \(\mathrm{tris}\)-chelate \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]^{3\oplus}}\) exists as a d/l pair, that the cis isomer of \(\mathrm{[PtCl_2(en)_2]^{2\oplus}}\) exists as a pair of enantiomers, and that square planar complexes do NOT show enantiomers because they possess a mirror plane and an axis of symmetry.

1. \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_2Cl_2]^{\oplus}}\) — an \(\mathrm{M(AA)_2B_2}\) octahedral complex, the same type as the worked \(\mathrm{[PtCl_2(en)_2]^{2\oplus}}\) case. Its cis form has no plane of symmetry and is chiral.

2. \(\mathrm{[Pt(en)Cl_2]}\) — four-coordinate platinum(II) with one bidentate en and two chlorides, i.e. a square planar complex. The molecular plane is itself a mirror plane, so it is achiral.

3. \(\mathrm{[Cr(C_2O_4)_3]^{3\ominus}}\) — a \(\mathrm{tris}\)-chelate of a bidentate oxalate ligand, structurally the same as \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]^{3\oplus}}\). The three chelate rings form a propeller which has a non-superimposable mirror image, so it is chiral.

4. \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2]^{\oplus}}\) — an \(\mathrm{MA_4B_2}\) complex containing only monodentate ligands. Both its cis and trans forms carry a mirror plane, so neither is chiral.

The chiral complexes are therefore 1 and 3.

First fix the oxidation state. Fluoride is \(-1\), so

\(x + 6(-1) = -3\), giving \(x = +3\), i.e. \(\mathrm{Cr^{3\oplus}}\).

Chromium is \(\mathrm{[Ar]3d^5 4s^1}\), so \(\mathrm{Cr^{3\oplus}}\) is a \(\mathrm{d^3}\) ion.

The chapter states that for the configurations \(\mathrm{d^1}\), \(\mathrm{d^2}\) and \(\mathrm{d^3}\) the electrons occupy the \(\mathrm{t_{2g}}\) orbitals and obey Hund's rule, and that only \(\mathrm{d^4}\) to \(\mathrm{d^7}\) give a high-spin/low-spin distinction. With three \(\mathrm{t_{2g}}\) orbitals available, the three electrons occupy them singly with parallel spins whatever the field strength — and fluoride is in any case a weak field ligand, low in the spectrochemical series given in the chapter.

So the arrangement is \(\mathrm{t_{2g}^3 e_g^0}\) with three unpaired electrons. One, two or four unpaired electrons would require a \(\mathrm{d}\) count other than three, which the \(+3\) oxidation state rules out.

The number of unpaired electrons is three.

Only the chloride ions in the IONISATION sphere — those written outside the square bracket — are free in solution and available to precipitate silver chloride. Chloride bound inside the coordination sphere is non-ionisable and gives no precipitate; the chapter's 'Remember' box makes the same point for \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]Cl_3}\), which yields three moles of \(\mathrm{AgCl}\).

One mole of \(\mathrm{AgCl}\) therefore means exactly ONE ionisable chloride. Counting the chloride outside the bracket in each choice gives 1, 2, 0 and 3 respectively.

Only \(\mathrm{[CoCl_2(NH_3)_4]Cl}\) has a single ionisable chloride, and it is consistent in the other respects too: cobalt is \(+3\) and the coordination number is six.

The formula of the complex is \(\mathrm{[CoCl_2(NH_3)_4]Cl}\).

Two quantities are needed.

Coordination number: the chapter defines it as the number of ligand DONOR atoms attached to the metal, not the number of ligands. Ethylenediamine is bidentate and oxalate is bidentate, so two en ligands contribute \(2 \times 2 = 4\) donor atoms and \(\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2\ominus}}\) contributes 2. Hence \(\mathrm{C.N.} = 6\).

Oxidation number: the chloride outside the bracket is the counter ion, so the complex ion is \(+1\). With en neutral and oxalate \(-2\),

\(x + 2(0) + (-2) = +1\), so \(x = +3\).

The sum is \(6 + 3 = 9\).

The alternatives 6, 7 and 8 would require the metal in the \(0\), \(+1\) and \(+2\) states, and none of those leaves the coordination sphere with the \(+1\) charge that the single chloride counter ion demands. Note also that counting the two en ligands as two rather than four donor atoms would give a coordination number of 4 and is the error the question is testing.

The sum of coordination number and oxidation number is 9.
